text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Scepticism rules after "tax summit" meeting between government and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) as both sides emphasise their current positions.
- Research Minister Juergen Ruettgers pledges people will not be cloned and calls for responsible handling of genetic engineering issues.
- Railway lines across Germany attacked by saboteurs. Police suspect anti-nuclear activists.
- Institute for Economic Research (IWH) in Halle predicts unemployment will rise this year in eastern Germany.
- East German members of parliament in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats plan to end their blockade on reforms to corporate tax.
HANDELSBLATT
- IG Metall and OeTV trade unions organise opposition to government tax reform plans.
- Volkswagen doubles group profits in 1996.
- Allianz posts 1996 pretax profits up more than 40 percent.
- Imports more expensive due to strong dollar.
- Regulator plans legal action to force Deutsche Telekom to open up Berlin cable network to other channels.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Violent protests against transport of nuclear waste.
- Ruling coalition agrees deserters from Soviet army and its allies can stay in Germany.
- Johannes Gerster quits as head of Christian Democrats in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's home state of Rhineland-Palatinate to take up job with Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Israel.
- Government plans to transfer 435,000 homes to private ownership in the coming years.
- Bavarian February inflation stagnates at 1.6 percent.
DIE WELT
- President Roman Herzog promises German support for Hungary in its bids for NATO and EU membership.
- Number of fatalities in German road accidents declines in 1996.
- Prospects for skilled crafts sector remain bleak, ZDH trade association says.
- SPD and government attempt to agree common calculations on tax reform.
